01.note: On another occasion Rabbi Yohanan came upon the young son of Reish Lakish, his late study partner, sitting and reciting a verse from Proverbs: a man's own foolishness ruins his path, and then his heart rages against God. Rabbi Yohanan wondered aloud whether this idea had any hint in the Torah itself. The boy answered at once with Genesis, where Joseph's brothers, in trouble, ask what God has done to them. Rabbi Yohanan raised his eyes and stared at him, and the boy's mother hurried him away, afraid Rabbi Yohanan would do to her son what he had done to his father.
01.why: It is a second tale about the same clever boy, following his exchange with Rabbi Yohanan about tithes; the Gemara then calls it a digression and returns to Rabbi Yohanan's teachings about rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Leading Sage of the Land of Israel; Reish Lakish was his study partner and brother-in-law.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's great study partner, already dead here; the boy's father.

terms.meaning: The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah (the Five Books of Moses) and the Prophets. It includes Psalms, Proverbs, Job and other books.

02.note: Rav Daniel bar Ketina owned a garden and walked through it every day to see what it needed. He would say: this bed needs water, and this bed does not. Then rain would come and water exactly the places that needed it, and nowhere else.
02.why: The Gemara has just read a verse from Zechariah to mean that rain can fall for a single person, a single field, even a single plant; Rav Daniel's garden shows it happening.

people.name: Rav Daniel bar Ketina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, remembered here for rain that fell only where his garden needed it.

03.note: Rabbi Abba the priest reported, in the name of Rabbi Yosei the priest, that the sons of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina died, and that throughout the seven days of mourning he bathed in cold water.
03.why: Rava has ruled that a mourner may bathe in cold water, and this report is offered as support. The Gemara turns it aside: his periods of mourning came one right after another, a case where the rules are eased anyway.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel whose sons died; the report concerns how he mourned them.

people.name: Rabbi Abba the priest
people.about: The Sage who passes the report on.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: The Sage in whose name the report is given.

terms.meaning: After a close relative dies, Jewish law sets a week of intense mourning (shiva) with restrictions on bathing, grooming and pleasures.

04.note: Rabbi Abbahu used to think he was humble, until he saw Rabbi Abba of Akko let his interpreter give a reason of his own in place of the one Rabbi Abba had given, and not mind at all. Rabbi Abbahu's own humility is then shown: his interpreter's wife told Rabbi Abbahu's wife that her husband did not really need Rabbi Abbahu, and bent down to hear him only out of courtesy. When his wife repeated this, Rabbi Abbahu asked what difference it made to her: through both of them, God above would be praised.
04.why: Rabbi Abbahu has just said he stopped reciting certain verses during the Priestly Blessing because Rabbi Abba of Akko did not; the Gemara adds his other remark about Rabbi Abba and opens a run of stories about his humility.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A leading Sage of Caesarea in the Land of Israel, with ties to the Roman authorities.

people.name: Rabbi Abba of Akko
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Abbahu admired for his humility.

terms.meaning: At a public lecture the Sage spoke quietly to an interpreter, who stood and repeated or expanded his words aloud for the crowd.

05.note: A man found pitch near a winepress and came to ask Rav what to do with it. Rav told him to take it for himself. Seeing the man still hesitate, Rav said: go and share it with my son Hiyya, showing he was sure it was not stolen property.
05.why: The discussion asks whether the place where an item is found counts as a mark that lets the owner reclaim it. Rav's ruling seems to say no, but Rabbi Abba explains it otherwise: grass had grown through the pitch, so its owner had long given up on it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the great academy at Sura in Babylonia, one of the most important early Sages of the Talmud.

people.name: Hiyya
people.about: Rav's son.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage who explains the reasoning behind Rav's ruling.

terms.meaning: A feature an owner can describe to prove a lost item is his. A finder must announce items that have one; items without one may often be kept.
Once an owner has given up hope of getting a lost item back, it becomes ownerless and the finder may keep it.

06.note: Rav borrowed gold dinars from the daughter of Rabbi Hiyya. By the time he came to repay, gold dinars had risen in value, and Rav worried that returning them would mean paying her interest. He went to Rabbi Hiyya, who told him: go and pay her back in good, full-weight dinars.
06.why: The Gemara is asking whether gold coins count as money or as goods compared with silver, and reads this ruling as showing Rabbi Hiyya treated gold as money. It then rejects the proof: Rav had dinars of his own elsewhere, which changes the case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the academy at Sura in Babylonia; he had studied in the Land of Israel and was related to Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Mishna, Rav's teacher and uncle.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a Jew to pay or take any extra on a loan to another Jew, including repaying goods that have gone up in value.
A measure of volume for grain and produce. Lending a se'a of produce and getting a se'a back is forbidden, because prices may rise in between.

07.note: Abba Mar, the son of Rav Pappa, used to accept pans of wax from wax makers and then ask his father to lend them money. The Sages complained to Rav Pappa that his son was taking interest. Rav Pappa replied that interest of this kind is fine: the Torah forbids only interest that passes from borrower to lender, and his son was simply being paid for putting in a word.
07.why: Rava has just ruled that a person may take a fee for asking someone else to make a loan; this case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Son of Rav Pappa, who earned wax for arranging loans from his father.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, head of an academy at Naresh.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a lender to take any extra from a Jewish borrower in return for a loan.

08.note: Rabbi Abba owed money to Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, and they came before the judge Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. Rabbi Abba said he would pay once he got his promissory note back; Rav Yitzhak said he had lost it and offered to write a receipt instead. Rabbi Abba cited Rav and Shmuel, who rule that no receipt is written. The judge said he honored Rav and Shmuel so much he would put their dust on his eyes, but Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish both rule that a receipt is written.
08.why: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said a receipt is never written when a whole debt is repaid; the Gemara disagrees and brings this case to prove that it is.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: The lender, who had lost the promissory note.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The borrower, who would not pay without getting the note back.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: The Sage who served as judge in the case.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: The two great early Sages of Babylonia, often cited as a pair.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
people.about: The two great Sages of the Land of Israel in their generation, study partners.

terms.meaning: A written loan document. Normally it is handed back or torn up when the debt is paid, so it cannot be used to collect a second time.
A signed document saying the debt was paid, written for the borrower when the note itself cannot be returned.

09.note: Two cases about repaying loans. In the first, a lender told a borrower to repay him in front of two named men, but the borrower repaid in front of two others. Abaye said two witnesses are two witnesses; Rava answered that naming them was meant to rule out exactly that. In the second, a lender asked to be repaid in front of two men learned in law, but the borrower paid him privately, and the money was later lost through no fault of the lender. The lender told Rav Nahman he had held it only for safekeeping until the condition was met. Rav Nahman ruled it a proper repayment: he and Rav Sheshet were learned men, so if the lender insisted on the condition, let him bring the money and be repaid before them.
09.why: Rava has just ruled on when a loan must be repaid in front of witnesses, and the Gemara now lists a series of real cases about loans, witnesses and repayment.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, often in debate with his colleague Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, Abaye's frequent debating partner.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A senior Babylonian Sage and judge, known for rulings on money law.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Babylonian Sage famed for his vast knowledge of earlier teachings.

terms.meaning: Property held for someone else. A person holding it for free is not liable if it is lost through events beyond his control.
Early collections of teachings from the time of the Mishna: Sifra and Sifrei explain biblical books verse by verse, and the Tosefta is a companion to the Mishna.

09.flag: The STORY segments join two separate loan cases (repaying before named witnesses, and before men learned in law) from a run of several such cases.

10.note: The Roman emperor Antoninus told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that he wanted two things: for his son Asveirus to rule after him, and for the city of Tiberias to be freed from taxes, but the Senate would grant only one request. Rabbi answered without words: he set one man on another's shoulders, gave the top man a dove, and told the bottom man to tell him to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask the Senate to make his son king, then have his son free Tiberias. When Antoninus complained that leading Romans were troubling him, Rabbi took him into his garden and each day pulled up a single radish. Antoninus understood: deal with them one at a time. Rabbi used signs because he feared the Romans would hear, even a whisper.
10.why: The Gemara has said that the Romans will crown a king's son if the king asks, naming Asveirus son of Antoninus; this story shows how that came about.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor whom the Talmud portrays as a close friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Leader of the Jews of the Land of Israel and editor of the Mishna, often called simply Rabbi.

people.name: Asveirus
people.about: Son of Antoninus, whom he wanted to succeed him.

terms.meaning: The council of Roman nobles whose approval the emperor needed for his requests.
